newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU moved to avert wheat market squeeze at tender.
newsitem.headline: EU moved to avert wheat market squeeze at tender.

text.p: The European Commission decided to grant more wheat than expected at Thursday's weekly export tender to act against an apparent squeeze on export licences, an EU official said on Friday.

"It was done to stop this situation. It will discourage people from squeezing the market so we can continue to cover short positions next week in normal conditions," the official, who is familiar with EU grain export policy, told Reuters.
"This does not mean that if people bid 20 Ecus we are going to cover," he added.

A stand-off between exporters over the control of export licences dominated Thursday's tender as traders with short positions scrambled to secure cover while a handful of companies sought the maximum advantage from long positions, traders said.

Speculation about a squeeze mounted after one company bid for 250,000 tonnes of export licences at low refunds in an apparent effort to discourage the Commission from accepting other bids for higher rebates, traders said.
Many traders are said to be short of EU licences and possibly facing losses of at least $15 a tonne on wheat sales to North Africa.

The Commission surprised the market, however, by setting its maximum refund at 10.25 Ecus per tonne -- well above the lowest refund bid of 6.77 Ecus, which implied a highly attractive EU fob price near $160, $10 per tonne above U.S. soft red winter wheat.
The highest refund given was valued at $156 a tonne.

The move reduced the market's short position, but at a loss to some traders. They had gambled on a rise in refunds before both a recovery in world markets and a sudden rise in the dollar put pressure on EU export subsidies.
Traders estimated the firm that placed the most competitive bids this week had seen a gap estimated at $1 million open up between the value of licences it took and the maximum award.
Traders at the company declined to comment.
In a parallel move, the European Commission unexpectedly dropped its EU wheat flour export refund below the underlying wheat grain refund in two stages this week.
The new flour refund of eight Ecus per tonne is 21 percent less than the latest maximum wheat grain refund, whereas in usual conditions it would be pegged around 37 percent higher.
The EU official said this was done to damp down a market that had seen significant demand for licences as the value of wheat refunds plunged on the secondary open market.
Flour export commitments were also well advanced, he said.
The result was a "non-operational" flour refund that would discourage normal bidding but would still leave scope for those who really needed to do business, he said.
Latest EU figures show July/June flour export commitments at 5.036 million tonnes up to March 4, member state officials said.
That figure is 44 percent up on the same point last year.
Soft wheat commercial grain export commitments are at 7.711 million tonnes, up 48 percent, plus the 436,500 tonnes of soft wheat that the Commission granted for export on Thursday.
-- Tim Hepher, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5146
